opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few things going on. The first is that when you look at how capabilities scale with compute, you tend to see something like smooth, roughly log-linear improvements on many benchmarks: each tenfold increase in compute buys you a fairly consistent chunk of improvement. On its face, that sounds like diminishing returns. You're pouring in exponentially more resources for roughly linear gains in some measured score.

But the mapping from benchmark performance to economic or practical value isn't linear, and it's especially non-linear around human-level performance. Think about what happens when a system goes from being able to do, say, 80% of the subtasks in a job to 95% or 100%. At 80%, you still need a human in the loop for the remaining pieces, and that human is often the bottleneck. You get some productivity boost, but the task still fundamentally depends on human labor. Once the system can reliably do the whole thing end to end, you can substitute rather than just complement. Then you can run as many copies as you have compute for, at whatever speed the hardware allows. That's a qualitative shift, not an incremental one.

There's a related point about the distribution of tasks in the economy. Many tasks cluster in a range of difficulty near what humans can do, because the economy is organized around human capabilities. So as systems cross that threshold, they don't unlock one task at a time. They can unlock a large mass of tasks over a relatively narrow band of capability improvement. A modest increase in effective capability translates into a big jump in the share of work that can be automated.

And then there's reliability. A lot of value depends on getting things right consistently, not just on average. Going from 90% to 99% to 99.9% reliability might look like small improvements on a chart, but each of those steps can open up entirely new categories of deployment where errors are costly.

Finally, there's a feedback element. If AI systems start contributing meaningfully to the things that drive further progress, like software engineering, research, or chip design, then the gains don't just add to output. They feed back into the rate of improvement itself. Even if raw capability grows roughly linearly in log-compute, the value can grow much faster than linearly, because you're crossing these thresholds of substitutability, task coverage, and reliability all at once in the region near human-level performance.

r001.rationale: The response describes nonlinear value near human-level capability in general, but does not explain the self-driving-car example or say that performing 10% worse than humans can cost disproportionately more than 10% of a human-level car’s value.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So I think the key thing to notice is that if you look at the raw benchmark numbers, or even something like loss on a next-token prediction task, you see these fairly smooth, kind of boring curves. Loss goes down roughly as a power law in compute, and if you plot it on a log scale it looks almost linear. So people look at that and say, well, we're putting in exponentially more compute and getting only linear improvements in loss, so this is a really inefficient process and surely it's going to peter out.

But I think that's confusing the measurement with the thing we actually care about. Loss, or accuracy on a benchmark, is not the same as economic value. And the mapping between the two is highly nonlinear, especially in the region right around human-level performance.

Here's one way to think about it. A lot of valuable tasks in the economy are things where you need to get a long chain of steps right. If you're writing a piece of software, or doing a multi-step research task, or handling a customer interaction end to end, you need to not make a mistake at step one, and step two, and step three, and so on. If your per-step reliability is, say, 90 percent, and the task has twenty steps, your chance of completing the whole thing is something like twelve percent. That's basically useless. Nobody will pay for that. Now bump the per-step reliability to 99 percent, and suddenly you're completing the task about 80 percent of the time. That's a tenfold improvement in a linear-ish measure of error, but it's taking you from "not usable" to "usable," which from an economic standpoint is a difference of many orders of magnitude.

So you have this threshold effect. Below a certain level of capability, the system can't substitute for a human at all, because the human needs to check every step and at that point you might as well have done it yourself. Above the threshold, you can delegate the entire task, and that unlocks the full wage of the human doing that work. The value doesn't scale smoothly with the benchmark score, it jumps when you cross the point where delegation becomes viable.

And there's a second mechanism, which is about the horizon of tasks. We've looked at this with the data from METR and others, where the length of task that models can do reliably has been roughly doubling every several months. If each doubling of compute lets you handle tasks that are, say, 50 percent longer, that doesn't sound dramatic. But the number of economically meaningful tasks that fit inside a given time horizon grows very quickly as the horizon expands. Tasks that take a human an hour are far more valuable and far more numerous in the economy than tasks that take a minute. So even a steady improvement in horizon length translates into a rapidly expanding share of the economy that's addressable.

Then the third piece is complementarity. Once you cross human-level on enough of the pieces, you stop being a tool that a human uses and you become something that can be composed with itself. You can run many copies, have them work in parallel, have them check each other's work. The marginal cost of an additional "worker" is just inference compute. So the value isn't just "one human-equivalent," it's whatever the returns are to having a large, cheap, scalable labor force that can be deployed on the problems with the highest returns, including improving the AI systems themselves.

So when you put those together, you get a picture where the inputs are growing exponentially, the intermediate metrics look like they're improving only modestly per doubling, but the economic output that depends on those metrics can grow superlinearly, because we're in the range where small improvements are flipping tasks from infeasible to feasible. I think a lot of the skepticism about scaling comes from looking at the wrong variable. If you look at loss, it looks like diminishing returns. If you look at what fraction of the economy's tasks a system can actually do end to end, I think it looks a lot more like we're approaching a steep part of the curve rather than flattening out.

r001.rationale: The response explains nonlinear value thresholds for multi-step tasks, but does not discuss self-driving cars or say that a car performing 10% worse than humans loses disproportionately more than 10% of its value.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that performance on a task and the economic value of that performance aren’t necessarily proportional. You might have a system that can do quite a lot of what a human does, but still needs enough supervision that it isn’t particularly useful as a substitute for human labor. As you close those remaining gaps, you can suddenly automate an entire task, and that can be much more valuable than making an assistant slightly better.

There’s also a complementarity between capabilities. If a system can write code but can’t reliably debug it or understand the requirements, its usefulness is limited. Improving those other capabilities makes its coding ability more valuable as well. So you’re not just adding up independent improvements; the improvements can reinforce each other.

Near human-level performance, you might cross a lot of these thresholds in a relatively small range of capability. So even if the underlying technical improvements are fairly smooth as you scale compute, the economic returns can rise quite sharply. That isn’t guaranteed by exponential compute growth alone—it depends on where those thresholds are and whether the systems are cheap and reliable enough to deploy.

r001.rationale: The response says small capability gaps can sharply reduce economic value, but it does not explain the self-driving-car example or state that being 10% worse than humans can cost more than 10% of the value of human-level performance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between performance on a task and the economic value of that performance. Those needn’t move together in a smooth, linear way. Going from being able to do 80% of a job to being able to do 100% can be much more valuable than that percentage improvement suggests, because you can now automate the whole job rather than requiring a human to supervise or finish it.

There are also complementarities between capabilities. If a system can write code but can’t debug it or work out what the user actually needs, its usefulness is constrained. As those other capabilities improve, the coding ability becomes more valuable too. So improvements across several dimensions can reinforce one another.

Near human-level performance, you might cross a lot of those thresholds in relatively quick succession. A system goes from being an occasionally useful assistant to being able to carry out substantial tasks independently. That creates the possibility of a very steep increase in economic value, even if the underlying improvements in measured capabilities look fairly gradual. It’s not guaranteed, but it’s a reason not to assume that smooth scaling curves imply smooth growth in economic impact.

r001.rationale: The response explains that a job’s value can rise disproportionately when performance improves from 80% to full completion, but it does not communicate the self-driving-car example or the specific claim about a 10% performance gap.
